items.title: Missing Authentication on /libp2p-http Ingress in Google OSS Agent Mesh (SAM)
items.summary: Classification: Critical, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Proof-of-Concept, CVSSv4.0: 9.3, CVEs: CVE-2026-102503, Summary: A SAM node exposes its registered backend services (MCP / A2A / inference, including command/stdio-backed MCP servers) over two libp2p paths. The MCP-protocol path is wrapped in WithBiscuitAuth -> Authorize, which enforces the node's biscuit policy (allowed_tools / allowed_targets). The parallel /libp2p-http ingress reaches the same backend service handlers with no authorization check at all. Any peer that can dial the node — no enrollment, no valid biscuit — invokes any registered backend tool, defeating the policy the project ships and tests as its core security boundary.

items.title: Agents are your newest insiders. Security must move at their speed.
items.summary: Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done. They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business. To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents. That access is what makes agents more capable. With that capability can come insider risk. This does not mean agents are inherently malicious. It means they are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems by users. They can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised. Their models can produce variable outputs, their context can change, and their plans can evolve as they work. An agent that operates as intended when a task begins may respond differently as context or inputs change. Depending on how they are designed and deployed, agents can operate continuously, at machine speed and scale. Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. We should not ask a model to be its own security authority. The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them.

items.title: Insecure Default Policy and Unrestricted OIDC Enrollment in Google OSS Agent Mesh (SAM)
items.summary: Classification: Critical, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Proof-of-Concept, CVSSv4.0: 9.3, CVEs: CVE-2026-103091, Summary: SAM's MCP proxy has no authorization. Any authenticated mesh member can invoke any tool on any node, with full read/write/exec on the backend. The only prerequisite is the control plane URL (via Shodan, I currently found a few via a header, but since this project is still in its very early adoption stage it makes sense the numbers aren't big right now, it's got like 700 stars on GH). From there, the control plane hands over everything needed to join the mesh.

items.title: PSA: Patch your Plex media server before someone hacks it
items.summary: Recently fixed vulnerabilities in the Plex Media Server are under active exploitation in attacks that, when successful, install malware, including cryptominers and residential proxy apps, a researcher said. Plex fixed four vulnerabilities at the start of last month. Three weeks later, published CVE designations revealed five vulnerabilities, with one of them carrying a severity rating of 8.6 out of a possible 10. A researcher last week revealed an exploit that chained four of them together to achieve remote code execution of the device running a vulnerable Plex version. The researcher named the chain “Plex2Shell.” The new details allowed a separate researcher to create a honeypot that could track attempts in the wild to exploit the vulnerability chain. Within a day, the researcher began seeing active scanning of the simulated Plex server and eventually successful attempts to infect devices. So far, successful attacks are installing two payloads. One is a cryptominer, which uses the device to mine cryptocurrency and deposit it into a wallet controlled by the attacker.

items.title: The Evolving Cybersecurity Lexicon: Vulnerability Discovery to Resilience
items.summary: Every year, the lexicographers at Merriam-Webster officially add new words or word usage to the dictionary. It's a fascinating process, outlined here. In 2009, a new usage of the word "tweet" was added to describe a social media post from the microblogging site then known as Twitter. "App" was added in 2010 to describe application software. And, in 2025, the word "slop" was amended to include AI slop, mass quantities of content created using generative AI. Watching our language and usage evolve gives us a glimpse into the zeitgeist. When we reflect on 2026 and cybersecurity, what will the word of the year be? Without a doubt, the word of 2026 will be "vulnerability" or its plural "vulnerabilities." Think back to RSAC 2026, when the consensus post-conference was that the industry is suffering in a sea of sameness, and cybersecurity is a mature market that will be consolidated, commoditized, and monitored as a cost center. Then, on April 7, 2026, along came the public disclosure of Anthropic's Claude Mythos, and the word "vulnerability" was the topic of conversation for everyone from CEOs to pundits to security researchers. The industry launched into a full fear, uncertainty, and doubt (FUD) campaign, with the "vulnpocalypse" being declared.

items.title: How a Massive Chinese Crime Ring Hacked Staples to Steal Millions
items.summary: A Chinese organized crime hacked into retail giant Staples, used that access to fraudulently issue millions of dollars worth of gift cards for stores like Target and Sephora, then went on a nationwide shopping spree, shipping many of the stolen electronics and other products back to China as part of a massive retail theft operation, 404 Media has learned. The finding, based on a review of court records, reveals the scale at which some organized crime groups are fleecing U.S. retailers, with entire warehouses dedicated to housing the merchandise. The hack of Staples, which has not been previously reported, signals just how sophisticated some of these operations have become. In October 2023, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) received information from an office supply company, saying that hackers had targeted the company and issued more than 15,000 gift cards worth over $5 million, according to a search warrant application unsealed last week. The document does not name the company, but 404 Media determined it was Staples based on various clues: the document says the victim company is headquartered in Massachusetts; uses a company called Blackhawk Network to fulfill its giftcard orders; and the hacked company has an internal customer support system called Nexus. All of those identifying features match Staples, and 404 Media found a reference to Nexus on a former Staple’s executive’s LinkedIn profile.

items.title: Linux KVM guest-host escape rated critical, may represent a new way to attack penguin-powered networking
items.summary: Paulos Yibelo, the researcher who in early October claimed to have found a guest-host escape flaw in Linux KVM, the hypervisor used by most hyperscale clouds, has named the flaw PwnEscape and warned it might represent a new way to attack Linux – on top of being a 9.3-rated critical nasty in its own right. Yibelo’s work is now CVE-2026-99999. It is a scary bug because it makes a guest-host escape possible with a few malformed IPv4 packets. Such attacks are a nightmare security scenario because the whole point of virtualization is carving up hardware into isolated “guest” virtual machines that share a “host” server’s resources – without ever being able to see what other guests or the host are doing. Public clouds rely on that isolation remaining impervious. So do private clouds, because if guest/host isolation is violated, an attacker could conceivably access all the VMs on a host or pool of virtualized hardware. Attacks on a host could give an evildoer access to thousands of VMs, plus containers because many developers now run those constructs in a micro-VM to keep them isolated.

items.title: Hackers hijack AOMEI update servers to secretly spread malware
items.summary: Hackers reportedly compromised AOMEI's servers to distribute malware through a built-in promotional feature in its backup software, briefly tampering with configuration files before restoring them to their original state to hide the attacks. The supply chain attacks took place between April and July 2026 and targeted the update and notification systems used by AOMEI Backupper, a Windows application for backing up data, cloning disks, and restoring systems. Researchers at ManageEngine's Threat Analysis Lab (METAL), working with Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, uncovered the campaign and investigated the attacks. In reports published by Google and ManageEngine, the activity is attributed to a threat actor tracked as UNC7017, who used the compromised infrastructure to distribute a previously unknown malware downloader called CROSSROAD and a backdoor named SHINYROAD. The researchers identified affected organizations in multiple countries, including the United States, Australia, India, Singapore, Spain, and Switzerland, across sectors such as IT services, telecommunications, and higher education.

items.title: Hackers steal customer data from major Russian hosting provider FirstVDS
items.summary: Hackers have stolen passwords, access credentials and other sensitive data belonging to customers of Russian hosting provider FirstVDS after exploiting a vulnerability in software used to manage its servers, the company said over the weekend. The attack, discovered on Saturday, affected part of FirstVDS's infrastructure, allowing the hackers to access data stored on customers' virtual servers without disrupting their operations. According to the company, the attackers exploited a vulnerability in VMmanager 6, a virtualization management platform developed by Russian software company ISPsystem. The platform allows hosting providers to manage virtual machines across multiple physical servers. The hackers then deployed malware that allowed them to copy data from customers' virtual servers, including passwords, cloud service credentials, configuration files, cryptocurrency wallets and other files. The stolen information was transferred to a server controlled by the attackers, according to FirstVDS. The company said the breach affected only some of its infrastructure but did not disclose how many customers or servers were compromised.

items.title: One Parser, Two Bugs, Many Routers: Exploiting Broadcom WiFi Across eCos and Linux
items.summary: A vulnerability affecting Broadcom’s proprietary implementation of 802.11 has been present in their SDK since at least 2010. An incomplete patch was silently released in 2018, followed by Broadcom’s recommendation to move to hostapd instead, making it a definitive forever day on eCos-based platforms (BCM3380, BCM3383, BCM33834) and a potential forever day on Linux platforms (BCM3390, BCM65xx, BCM68xx) unless affected Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) are willing to migrate. The vulnerability can be triggered remotely over WiFi without knowledge of the network key or completion of a normal WPS enrollment. Exploitation provides controlled information disclosure and arbitrary code execution. It affects dozens of vendors, hundreds of products, and millions of Broadcom-based access points worldwide. In an effort to discover all affected vendors and devices, I’m providing a fingerprinting script and YARA rule so you can help me document the blast radius. According to Broadcom’s own response, they’ve known about the bug since 2018 and they’ve received information about it from other external entities. Yet they refused to assign a CVE to this vulnerability or to communicate publicly about it which is probably the reason why so many OEMs did not patch

items.title: Bullhorn takes staffing platform offline to contain cyberattack
items.summary: Staffing software company Bullhorn has disabled access to its platform to contain a cyberattack that caused a system-wide outage. The company says it has isolated the issue and eradicated the immediate threat. Currently, its team is working to restore services following thorough security reviews conducted with help from CrowdStrike specialists. Bullhorn is an American software company specializing in cloud-based staffing and recruitment solutions. Its platform helps staffing firms manage the recruitment lifecycle, including candidate tracking, onboarding, and payroll. The company says it serves more than 10,000 customers worldwide. According to a status page on the incident, customers started to experience issues with job posting in the Bullhorn application on Friday. The next day, the company said it was "experiencing a system-wide outage affecting the Bullhorn platform," and later confirmed that the issues were caused by a cyberattack."We have detected a cyber incident on the Bullhorn Platform. We have temporarily disabled access to our systems in order to contain the activity while we investigate further," the company said in an update.

items.title: OpenCode Console Breach May Have Exposed OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google API Keys
items.summary: An intruder reached a legacy system at OpenCode on the night of October 16 and may have exposed the third-party AI provider keys that users had saved in OpenCode Console, the company said. Console is OpenCode's optional hosted service: a workspace saves its own OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google key there, and Console uses that key to call the provider so team members can use the models without ever seeing the key. The affected group is 1.4% of Console users, all of whom have an outside provider linked, and OpenCode has told them via email to revoke those keys with each provider and replace them. The email went out on the morning of October 17 under the subject line "Action Required: Potential provider key breach." Anyone who did not get one was not affected, OpenCode said in a post on X later that day. The keys at risk are the ones pasted into Console. The OpenCode command-line and desktop apps keep provider keys added on the machine in a SQLite database there. The breach involves "the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself," co-founder Dax Raad wrote in a reply on X, and those keys "never come to us."

items.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
items.summary: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom. Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year. U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
